summary: This document gives functional requirements for supporting the Metro Ethernet Forum E-Tree service in multipoint Layer 2 VPN solutions. Future solutions are meant to use these requirements as guidelines.

plainLanguage.summary: In a tree-shaped network, leaves may talk to the root but not to each other. This lists what a private-network service needs to do to support that.

subtitle: Requirements for tree-shaped ethernet networks in virtual private networks.

tldr.problem: Service providers use Virtual Private LAN Service (VPLS) to offer Metro Ethernet Forum (MEF) Ethernet LAN services, which provide any-to-any connectivity. However, many customers need E-Tree services, where some endpoints (Leaves) can communicate with central endpoints (Roots) but not with each other—a tree-shaped topology VPLS does not natively support.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines functional requirements that solutions must meet to support E-Tree in Layer 2 VPN technology: prohibiting communication between Leaf endpoints, supporting multiple Roots, allowing Roots and Leaves to coexist, and maintaining backward compatibility with existing VPLS services.
tldr.outcome: By establishing clear requirements, this document guides the development of protocols and implementations that allow service providers to offer tree-shaped virtual networks alongside existing mesh networks, enabling more efficient support for hub-and-spoke configurations, mobile networks, video delivery, and other tree-structured use cases.

today: RFC 7152 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains the definitive requirements document for E-Tree support in L2VPN technologies. Various implementations of VPLS and E-VPN have since incorporated E-Tree functionality guided by these requirements.

sections.title: Introduction: E-LAN and E-Tree Services
sections.content:
MEF (Metro Ethernet Forum) defines two multipoint ethernet services: E-LAN (Ethernet LAN) and E-Tree (Ethernet Tree). E-LAN provides multipoint-to-multipoint connectivity where any endpoint can communicate with any other endpoint—like a traditional Ethernet network. E-Tree provides rooted-multipoint connectivity where the service has a tree structure: some endpoints are Roots that can communicate with any other endpoint, and some are Leaves that can communicate only with Roots.

Service providers currently use VPLS (Virtual Private LAN Service) over IP/MPLS networks to emulate E-LAN services. However, VPLS provides any-to-any connectivity among all endpoints and has no mechanism to restrict Leaf-to-Leaf communication, making it unsuitable for E-Tree services. This RFC defines the requirements that new L2VPN solutions must meet to support E-Tree.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two types of ethernet networks. One type (E-LAN) lets any office talk to any other office. The other type (E-Tree) has a tree shape: the head office talks to any branch, but branches should not talk to each other directly.

sections.title: E-Tree Concepts and Differences from E-LAN
sections.content:
E-LAN and E-Tree are similar in many ways: both use Ethernet frames, both forward based on MAC addresses, and both are bidirectional. The critical difference is in endpoint roles. In E-LAN, all endpoints are essentially equal (all are Roots). In E-Tree, each endpoint is designated either a Root or a Leaf. A Root can communicate with all other endpoints—other Roots and all Leaves. A Leaf can communicate only with Roots; it cannot communicate with other Leaves. This enforces a tree structure.

Within a generic E-Tree service, the following traffic flows are allowed: Ethernet unicast from Root to Leaf, from Leaf to Root, and from Root to Root; Ethernet broadcast and multicast from Root to other Roots and Leaves; and Ethernet broadcast and multicast from Leaf to Roots. A specific E-Tree service may support all these flows or only a subset depending on its application.
sections.plainLanguage: In E-Tree, you mark some connections as Roots and some as Leaves. Roots can talk to anything. Leaves can only talk to Roots, not to each other. This makes a tree shape.

sections.title: E-Tree Use Cases
sections.content: E-Tree services have many practical applications. Hub-and-spoke VPNs use a central hub site (Root) that communicates with multiple spoke sites (Leaves); the spokes do not need to communicate directly. Wholesale access connects a customer's interconnect point (Root) to multiple subscriber locations (Leaves). Mobile backhaul connects a Radio Access Network controller (Root) to multiple base stations (Leaves) that relay traffic through the controller. Precision Time Protocol clock synchronization uses a PTP time server (Root) sending synchronized time to multiple PTP clients (Leaves). Broadband internet access connects a broadband gateway (Root) to multiple subscriber premises (Leaves). Broadcast video sends video from a source (Root) to subscribers (Leaves) unidirectionally. Broadcast and multicast video adds a control channel for video selection. Device management connects a management system (Root) to managed devices (Leaves). In all these cases, direct Leaf-to-Leaf communication is either not required or must be prevented for security or operational reasons.
sections.plainLanguage: A bank has a head office (Root) and branches (Leaves). A phone company has a controller (Root) and cell towers (Leaves). A video company has servers (Root) and viewers (Leaves). All these are tree shapes.

sections.title: The VPLS Problem and Solution Requirement
sections.content:
VPLS was designed as a multipoint-to-multipoint service where all attachment circuits (ACs) are treated equally. It provides any-to-any connectivity with no mechanism for communication restriction between specific ACs. When VPLS is used to emulate an E-Tree service, a problem arises: when a Provider Edge (PE) router receives a frame from another PE over the pseudowire, it does not know whether the ingress AC on the source PE is a Leaf or Root. Therefore, it cannot enforce the Leaf-to-Leaf communication restriction. For example, if a Leaf sends a broadcast or multicast frame, a PE receiving it would forward it to all endpoints, including other Leaves, violating the E-Tree restriction. Similarly, if a Leaf unicast frame arrives with a destination MAC of another Leaf, a PE would forward it rather than blocking it.

To solve this problem, L2VPN solutions need the ability to identify which AC is the ingress AC and whether it is a Leaf or Root, so they can enforce communication restrictions accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: When a message arrives from another location, routers do not know if it came from a Leaf or a Root. If it is from a Leaf and heading to another Leaf, they should block it. But they do not know, so they forward it anyway.

sections.title: Functional Requirements for E-Tree Support
sections.content: RFC 7152 establishes three core functional requirements that any E-Tree L2VPN solution must meet. First, a solution MUST prohibit communication between any two Leaf ACs in an L2VPN instance. This is the defining characteristic of E-Tree: Leaf-to-Leaf traffic must be blocked or never sent. Second, a solution MUST allow multiple Root ACs in an L2VPN instance. Many use cases require redundancy, where multiple Root sites provide backup if the primary Root fails. Third, a solution MUST allow a Root AC and Leaf AC of the same L2VPN instance to coexist on the same PE router. In practical deployments, a single PE router may have both Root and Leaf endpoints connected. Solutions SHOULD minimize the impact on existing VPLS and E-VPN services, especially for MEF E-LAN services already in operation, and SHOULD be backward compatible with existing L2VPN solutions, allowing both legacy and new PEs to participate in a single L2VPN instance with Leaf-to-Leaf restrictions enforced only among compliant PEs.
sections.plainLanguage: Solutions must do three things: block Leaf-to-Leaf messages, allow multiple Roots, and let a PE have both Roots and Leaves. They should also still work with old services that do not use this feature.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content: The core requirement of prohibiting Leaf-to-Leaf communication exists partly for security reasons. In some E-Tree use cases, the restriction prevents unauthorized direct communication between endpoints that should only communicate through a central authority. For example, in a bank's branch network, the head office (Root) might apply policies or logging to all inter-site traffic; if branches could talk directly, they would bypass these controls. In a cellular network, a base station (Leaf) is designed to communicate through the RAN controller (Root), not directly with other base stations. The RFC notes that beyond this fundamental requirement, there are no additional security considerations beyond those already described in VPLS and E-VPN standards, which address topics like authentication of control-plane messages, data encryption, and access control lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you want Leaves to only talk through the Root for security or control reasons. That is why E-Tree exists. The usual network security rules still apply too.

left.title: E-LAN
left.desc: Any endpoint can communicate with any other endpoint.

right.title: E-Tree
right.desc: Roots can talk to anyone. Leaves can talk only to Roots.
